title-group.article-title: PlantAMP: A fine-tuned protein large language model for plant antimicrobial peptide prediction

body.p: Plant antimicrobial peptides (PAMPs) are small bioactive molecules with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, low toxicity, and roles in promoting plant growth, making them promising candidates for applications in sustainable agriculture and translational medicine (Nagella et al., 2025). However, PAMP discovery is constrained by the requirement for labor-intensive wet-lab validation and by the limitations of computational AMP predictors, which often rely on handcrafted features, shallow embeddings, fixed-length sequences, or intensive computation, thereby reducing their accuracy and generalizability in real-world settings (Qin et al., 2025).

Despite the emergence of models such as TriStack, LMPred, PAMPred, Diff-AMP, and AMPpred-MFA, large language model (LLM)-based strategies specifically designed for PAMP prediction remain rare (Wang et al., 2023, 2024; Han et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). Transformer-based models such as PCLPAMP suggest that protein sequences encode contextual patterns akin to natural language; however, transferring general pretraining often introduces biases and objective mismatches that hinder downstream performance (Qin et al., 2025).

In the present study, we present PlantAMP (Figure 1), a PAMP classifier built through prompt-guided fine-tuning of ProteinBERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers [BERT]), enabling task-specific representation learning without full model retraining (Brandes et al., 2022). Our strategy integrates stratified cross-validation, Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout)–based test-time augmentation, and a weighted ensemble to enhance robustness and generalizability (Lemay et al., 2022).Figure 1
Schematic overview of the PlantAMP workflow.
The framework comprises three key stages: data aggregation, ProteinBERT invocation, and model fine-tuning.
(A) Architecture of ProteinBERT: adapted from the original BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) design, PlantAMP processes sequences through two parallel branches: local (left) and global (right). Six transformer-style blocks alternately refine these representations via fully connected and convolutional sublayers, with residual connections and layer normalization. Global attention modules allow local features to contribute to the global embedding.
(B) PAMP (plant antimicrobial peptide) dataset assembly: experimentally validated PAMP sequences were compiled from published studies and public AMP (antimicrobial peptide) databases. After merging and deduplication, 2497 unique PAMPs were retained as positive samples, along with 2677 non-PAMPs as negative controls.
(C) Starting from the pretrained ProteinBERT encoder, we first froze the backbone and fine-tuned the classification head for five epochs at a learning rate of 1 × 10−3, then unfroze all layers for an additional 2 epochs at a reduced learning rate of 5 × 10−5, followed by a final tuning epoch at 2.5 × 10−5. At each training stage, dropout (rate = 0.3) and early stopping (patience = 1) were applied. For inference, we performed 50 stochastic forward passes with MC Dropout (Monte Carlo Dropout; rate = 0.3) under five-fold cross-validation and then ensembled predictions by weighting each fold’s output according to its validation MCC. Finally, classification thresholds were scanned from 0.30 to 0.70 in increments of 0.005 to maximize MCC. Model performance was evaluated on the test set using AUC, ACC, precision, recall, F1 score, and MCC. AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; ACC, accuracy; MCC, Matthews correlation coefficient.

PlantAMP consistently outperforms recent benchmarks in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), accuracy (ACC), precision, recall, F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), while reducing computational burden. Beyond its role as a model, it offers a scalable blueprint for adapting LLMs to peptide-discovery applications—using prompts to target semantics, efficient tuning to reduce costs, and ensembles to capture uncertainty. This generalizable framework can accelerate PAMP identification, and it can also be extended to other classes of bioactive peptides, enabling improvements in crop protection and therapeutic discovery (Wang et al., 2023; Nagella et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025).

To ensure that downstream modeling captured functional rather than dataset-specific artifacts, we first examined the sequence landscape. PAMP and non-PAMP sequences exhibited comparable length distributions—predominantly in the range of 30–150 amino acids, covering about 80% of all sequences—indicating that the discriminative signals were not length driven (Supplemental Figures 1A–1C). We then analyzed global amino acid composition and positional frequencies (Supplemental Figures 1D–1F). PAMPs were enriched in Cys residues (which support disulfide-stabilized cyclic motifs) and also exhibited clusters of basic residues, consistent with known electrostatic features linked to antimicrobial activity. In contrast, non-PAMPs displayed patterns typical of general proteins, transmembrane segments, and signal peptides (Supplemental Figure 2). These consistent distinctions indicate that class separability is underpinned by physicochemical preferences, not trivial length differences, supporting the validity of supervised modeling (Wang et al., 2023, 2024).

We next assessed PlantAMP, a fine-tuned LLM, using six metrics: AUC, ACC, precision, recall, F1 score, and MCC. On the held-out test set, PlantAMP achieved an AUC of 0.9766 and an area under the precision recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.9758, indicating strong separability despite class imbalance (Supplemental Figures 3A and 3B). Confusion matrix analysis confirmed high-fidelity PAMP identification with balanced false positive and false negative rates (Supplemental Figure 3C). Five-fold cross-validation yielded stable per-fold performance, indicating strong generalizability. Although 10-fold cross-validation offered slight improvements, the added training time outweighed the gains; therefore, we used five-fold cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol (Supplemental Table 1). Collectively, the compositional analyses and predictive benchmarks demonstrate that PlantAMP effectively learns PAMP-specific physicochemical signals and enables accurate, robust, and computationally efficient identification.

To compare PlantAMP with current methods, we benchmarked it against representative state-of-the-art PAMP/AMP predictors, including PCLPAMP, the LMPred variants (T5XL-BFD, T5XL-UNI, and BERT), Veltri-DNN, AmPEP, TriStack, AMPlify, AMPScanner (Vr1-RF, Vr1-Earth Precision, and Vr2), and TriNet (Brandes et al., 2022; Han et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). All models were retrained locally, starting from their official implementations and using the same curated dataset with unified preprocessing and consistent evaluation splits. Performance was assessed using AUC, ACC, precision, recall, F1 score, and MCC (Supplemental Figures 4A and 4B).

PlantAMP achieved the strongest overall performance, leading in four key metrics: AUC (0.9766), ACC (0.9235), precision (0.9419), and F1 score (0.9187). These results indicate strong class separability and effective precision–recall balancing despite class imbalance. Although PCLPAMP slightly outperformed PlantAMP in MCC (0.8516 vs. 0.8475), its lower AUC and F1 score indicated less consistent performance (Qin et al., 2025). TriStack, the strongest traditional machine learning/deep learning baseline, attained the highest recall (0.9436), but its AUC, precision, and F1 score lagged behind (Han et al., 2024). AMPScanner-Vr2 also prioritized recall at the expense of ACC and precision. Other baselines, including LMPred variants, AMPlify, Veltri-DNN, AmPEP, and AMPScanner-Vr1, underperformed relative to PlantAMP across most metrics (Supplemental Figures 4C and 4D).

These comparisons indicate that PlantAMP’s prompt-guided fine-tuning enables robust generalization with high computational efficiency (Supplemental Figures 5 and 6). By consistently ranking first or near the top across diverse evaluation criteria—particularly AUC, ACC, and precision—PlantAMP establishes a strong benchmark for PAMP identification. Moreover, its lightweight tuning framework offers a practical strategy for adapting protein LLMs to peptide-level tasks, outperforming handcrafted or conventional deep learning models while maintaining a favorable balance between sensitivity and reliability.

The performance of PlantAMP was validated through comparative analyses. We next evaluated whether PlantAMP learns task-relevant representations that distinguish PAMPs from non-PAMPs. Unsupervised projections of pretrained ProteinBERT embeddings, PlantAMP training-set embeddings, and PlantAMP test-set embeddings revealed a clear progression. The original feature space showed extensive class overlap, which indicates low separability. Fine-tuning with PlantAMP yielded distinct clusters in both training and test embeddings, with boundaries especially clear along the second projection axis. Silhouette scores significantly improved after fine-tuning, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p < 0.001) confirmed enhanced cluster separation, which supports the visual observation of coherent, class-consistent manifolds (Supplemental Figure 7).

We compared three ProteinBERT adaptation strategies using identical data splits and hyperparameters: full-model fine-tuning (all transformer layers and a classifier), BitFit-based tuning (bias-only updates with small prompts), and LoRA-based tuning (rank-four adapters in the attention and feedforward layers). Full-model tuning (PlantAMP) outperformed both lightweight variants on AUC (0.9766), ACC (0.9235), recall (0.8966), F1 (0.9187), and MCC (0.8475), though with slightly lower precision (0.9419). BitFit and LoRA reduced the training time by ∼50% and the parameter count by >70% but underperformed on five of six metrics (Supplemental Figure 8; Supplemental Table 2). Therefore, PlantAMP uses full fine-tuning to ensure predictive reliability, whereas prompt-based methods are more suitable for resource-limited scenarios (Brandes et al., 2022; Lemay et al., 2022).

Ablation experiments showed consistent drops in performance when omitting MC Dropout, ensembling, threshold tuning, freeze–unfreeze schedules, or dropout optimization (Lemay et al., 2022). MCC was particularly sensitive, decreasing from 0.8475 to 0.7999 without MC Dropout and to 0.8306 when a single model was used instead of an ensemble (Supplemental Figure 9).

ProteinBERT was selected for its residue-aware, parameter-efficient design, which enables stable fine-tuning on limited PAMP data. Comparative evaluations with ESM2 and ProtT5 confirmed PlantAMP’s superior performance, especially for AUC, validating this model choice (Supplemental Figure 10; Supplemental Table 3) (Brandes et al., 2022; Elnaggar et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2025).

PAMPs are low-toxicity agents with strong potential for applications in sustainable agriculture and translational medicine. In this study, we curated a large, non-redundant collection of 2497 experimentally validated PAMPs and 2677 length-matched non-PAMPs from six public resources (APD3, DBAASP, DRAMP, PlantPepDB, dbAMP, and NCBI) and developed PlantAMP, a ProteinBERT-based predictor fine-tuned using stratified cross-validation, MC Dropout ensembling, and validation-optimized decision thresholds. PlantAMP achieved robust performance on independent test data, which were split 5:1 into training (4311) and test (863) sets (Supplemental Table 4). When systematically screened against multiple AMP databases and the literature, its top-ranked predictions frequently aligned with experimentally validated AMPs (Wang et al., 2016; Sayers et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2025). Using full ProteinBERT adaptation, lightweight ensemble heads, and data-driven threshold optimization, this end-to-end framework improves generalization relative to handcrafted feature-based baselines, provides a scalable tool for PAMP prioritization, and lays a foundation for future motif-informed interpretability and structure-guided peptide engineering in sustainable agriculture and translational medicine (Brandes et al., 2022; Lemay et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2025).
